sections.heading: 2.1 Falsehoods
sections.text: Smith et al. (2025) discuss several conceptual problems with detecting deception from language models. In this work, we avoid many, but not all, of those problems by instead aiming to detect knowing falsehoods . That is, we wish to identify when an LLM makes a statement it believes to be false. We do not aim to detect deceptive intent, misleading but true statements, or any other type of non-falsehood-stating behavior. Nonetheless, as we show, detecting falsehoods still allows us to catch many of the most salient misaligned behaviors under monitoring. More formally, we define a transcript $T$ as containing a knowing falsehood for a model $M$ if it satisfies the following. Firstly, the final assistant response to the user in $T$ , denoted $r$ , must contain a set of asserted statements, each with a truth value, which we denote $\cal S$ . Secondly, for at least one of the statements $s\in\cal S$ , the model must believe that $s$ is false, which we denote $\operatorname{Bel}_{M}(\neg s\mid C)$ , where the context $C$ is the prefix of $r$ in $T$ . 1 1 1 Under our definition, a knowing falsehood can be objectively true. Reasoning is part of $C$ , not of $r$ . It is difficult to say in general whether a model believes something. Previous work has generally relied either on an appeal to common sense, or using the generations $y$ from $M$ given contexts related to $C$ , which we write $y\mid x$ for a context $x$ . For the purposes of this work, we say that a model $M$ believes a statement $s$ in context $C$ , i.e. $\operatorname{Bel}_{M}(s\mid C)$ , when any of the following is true: (1) Contextual evidence. $C$ contains clear evidence for $s$ , e.g. a tool result in $C$ stating $s$ . (2) Neutral elicitation. $C$ contains some pressure or incentive $P$ that we expect from the training procedure of $M$ to cause $y\mid C$ to contain $\neg s$ , while $y\mid\tilde{C}$ contains $s$ with high probability; here $\tilde{C}$ is $C$ with the minimal change to remove $P$ , and there is no competing incentive in $\tilde{C}$ (e.g. (3)). (3) Training-instilled belief. The model $M$ is known to achieve low loss on a training corpus where internalizing that $s$ is true is necessary to achieve this loss. This could be during pretraining by the developer, or as a post-training stage conducted by a model organism researcher. We say that a falsehood is contextual if belief is established via criterion 1, noting that in those cases the transcript alone determines if a falsehood is present, and otherwise it is introspective . We further distinguish cases of (3) where $s$ is a well-known fact, such that we can essentially not worry about what model $M$ is, and refer to this as pseudo-contextual .

sections.heading: 2.2 Training probes and monitors
sections.text: It is much easier to construct large datasets of contextual (or at least pseudo-contextual ) falsehoods than introspective ones, as the label is independent of the model and thus the dataset can be re-used over models. Similarly, no elicitation is required to verify a (competent) model’s beliefs for each dataset example. We therefore ask whether a large and sufficiently diverse set of contextual falsehoods, used to train expressive probes, can yield competitive monitors for real-world deployment, such as in frontier-scale sabotage detection, and whether such monitors can generalize to introspective cases. Our probes are classifiers $f:\mathbb{R}^{d|R|}\to[0,1]$ from hidden states $h\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for a set of read-out states $R$ , where the goal is for $f=1$ for falsehoods and 0 otherwise, trained on labeled data $\{h(C,r),\ell(C,r)\}$ , where the ground truth is determined from context alone. When scaling the training data, the full set is usually the union of multiple data sources $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\cup_{i=0}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{i}$ . There are then two ways to scale the training data: diversity , by increasing $N$ , and raw quantity , by increasing the size of each $\mathcal{D}_{i}$ . More generally, a monitor is any trusted system that serves to flag specific behaviors in another, usually more powerful, model. The most powerful black-box monitors have access to the hidden reasoning, known as CoT monitors, and thus could detect intent before the dangerous action is selected. Whereas, we focus on the more narrowly scoped action-only monitors , in anticipation of future models losing CoT monitorability (cf. § 1 ). We study monitors in a setting where an untrusted model is deployed as an agent in an environment where it can access tools, potentially allowing it to take unauthorized, dangerous actions in the real world. Each assistant turn $a_{i}$ is made up of many iterations of reasoning, tool call, and response. We call each of these a “step”, and use our probes, combined with a specific follow-up question, as monitors to detect if a misaligned action was taken in a particular step.

sections.heading: 4.1 The fibs dataset
sections.text: To investigate the effect of diversity and data scale in lie detector training, we create Falsehoods in Broad Settings ( fibs ), a contextual deception dataset of 163,016 transcripts, labeled by whether they contain knowing falsehoods (§ 2.1 ). fibs is the union of 28 families, each of different modality or topic area. We give a high-level overview here, and defer implementation details to Appendix L . Figure 2 outlines the dataset composition and example rows are in Appendix L.3 . A large fraction (76% of rows, 19 of 28 families) of the dataset is constructed synthetically from existing datasets with appended follow-up questions. For example, one family starts from MASK ( Ren et al., 2025 ) , where each example is a user-assistant chat with a designated truthful or deceptive answer. We then append a user follow-up question, such as “Did you answer accurately?”. The assistant response can be either “Yes” or “No”. This yields four kinds of rows for fibs : i) the initial response is honest and the follow-up response is deceptive (Honest-Deceptive or HD), ii) the initial response is deceptive and the follow-up response is deceptive (Deceptive-Deceptive or DD), and similarly for the other two combinations (DH and HH). In practice, we vary the follow-up question over a large set of fixed questions and responses, and sometimes generate follow-up questions and responses from another LLM. The next largest fraction of rows (18% of rows, 5 families) consist of on-policy examples from various models (§ L.1 ). Since models rarely spontaneously deceive, we use a variety of settings. Firstly, we run on-policy deception games using the harness from Golechha and Garriga-Alonso (2025) . Secondly, we use instructions or pressure to lie to the user, both in the system prompt and user turn. Finally, we leverage personas ( Marks et al., 2026 ) by generating a long transcript where the assistant acts disreputably and then generating the final turn on-policy, which frequently leads to a lie. In these families we also generate off-policy rows, so that on-policyness cannot be used as a shortcut for the probe. The final set of rows (6% of rows, 4 families) cover bespoke cases not covered in other families, such as assistants misrepresenting tool calls from earlier in the conversation, extremely long-context examples, direct false statements with no follow-up, etc. We validate labels through extensive LLM-as-a-judge filtering and estimate the label noise rate is $1.4\%\pm 0.1$ . This rate is measured against a “ground truth” evaluation from Claude Fable 5 given a dataset-agnostic definition of contextual falsehood similar to that in § 2.1 (Appendix L.6 ). We also balance the dataset exactly by label, control for the confounders of length and message count, and cap families at a size of 8,000 rows to ensure balance between settings. Although we believe fibs is currently the largest and most diverse falsehood dataset, it has several limitations. Firstly, few rows contain reasoning (only 5.5% of rows across only 6 families), as most examples come from non-reasoning models. Secondly, the dataset is entirely off-policy for almost all models we probe, except for Qwen3.5-122B, which generated 3% of fibs rows. Finally, the dataset is largely artificial. One family consists of transcripts from UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) with follow-up questions, but otherwise the dataset consists entirely of relatively simple evaluations or settings that are unrealistic for frontier model deployment.

sections.heading: 4.2 Scaling probes
sections.text: The most well-studied form of activation probe is the linear probe, a simple logistic regression on the residual stream at a single layer and token. Linear probes can be scaled along two axes: (i) more capacity , meaning more parameters, and (ii) greater input span , expanding the set of input activations $R$ (§ 2.2 ). For a higher capacity probe with the same single layer/token span as the linear probe, we use an MLP probe, a two-layer perceptron of hidden width 256. For these single-span probes, we train a probe per layer and average across all layers whose training loss is below 0.6, following Taufeeque et al. (2026) (Appendix A.2 ); we call the resulting per-layer ensembles the LinearEnsemble and MLPEnsemble probes. Our medium-capacity, long-span probe is the EFC probe (early-fusion covariance), adapted from Dooms et al. (2026) . At each token it concatenates activations across layers, projects them to a small dimension, and aggregates across tokens using the mean and covariance of the projected vectors; the output is a linear projection of those moments. The projections are parameterized and learnable. Our high-capacity, long-span probe is the axial probe, a small transformer where each block attends first across tokens, causally, and then bidirectionally across layers; the name refers to this axial factorization of attention. This probe has the fewest inductive biases of the four, not imposing any a-priori expectations about how concepts may be represented in activations. Probe implementation details are given in Appendix A . Table 1 in Appendix A.5 compares the parameter counts. Appendix A.6 expands on the training objective, optimizer parameters and the hyperparameter search behind it (the selected grid cells: Table 2 ). Across all four architectures, we use activations from six layers spread evenly from 30% to 90% of the model’s depth. For the axial and EFC probes, we use activations from the tokens of the final user and assistant turn. For the MLPEnsemble and LinearEnsemble probe we use just the last non-end-of-turn token. At evaluation time, we often prefill the final turn; e.g., user: “Did you respond truthfully?”, assistant: “Yes.”. This lets us remove any context-specific bias in probe scores by using the contrast score, i.e. the probe-score difference between “Yes.” and “No.” prefills. As a non-probe baseline we use the model’s self-report logit : the log-probability of the admitting reply minus that of the denying reply (e.g. $\log p(\texttt{No})-\log p(\texttt{Yes})$ after “Did you respond truthfully?”).

sections.heading: 4.3 Agentic setting: SHADE-Arena
sections.text: SHADE-Arena ( Kutasov et al., 2025 ) places an agent in a tool-using environment with a benign main task. In the side-task condition the agent is also instructed to complete a hidden side task the user did not ask for; in the honest condition it receives the main task only. An episode is one run of the agent loop, and its transcript is the resulting sequence of steps ; each step is reasoning ending in a tool call, plus that call’s result. We run our models on fourteen of 25 possible scenarios, and read the probes of § 4.2 from the same model’s residual stream. Appendix entries B.1 and C describe the scenarios and generation settings, including details on why some scenarios were discarded. Appendix Transcript H.2 shows a side-task step and an honest step. We collect 25 rollouts per scenario and condition. By default, SHADE-Arena does not provide a robust way to identify whether a given action contributes (ideally exclusively) toward the main-task or side-task. As such, to evaluate our probes as action monitors, we used an LLM judge (Claude Haiku 4.5 2 2 2 We compare its labels with those of other LLM judges on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B rollouts of all 25 scenarios (Appendix B.5 , Table 4 ). ) to generate per-step labels, as detailed in Appendix K.1 . The first step the judge marks as pursuing the side task is the side task’s onset ; steps of a side-task episode from the onset on are the positive class, and its earlier steps and every step of an honest episode are the negative class (Figure 4(c) ). Appendix B.4 details the per-step labels. The 14 scenarios are those left after we drop 11 in which a judge cannot tell side-task work from main-task work in a single step (Appendix B.1 ). On Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, they give 699 scored episodes, with 5,014 positive and 16,275 negative steps. To evaluate our probes as action monitors, we prefill follow-up questions (§ 4.2 ) after every tool-call, following Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) . The assistant’s “yes” or “no” response is prefilled with empty reasoning, and previous pre-tool reasoning blocks are automatically removed by the Qwen3.5 chat template — so our probes do not monitor the chain-of-thought. We test three follow-ups, increasing in scenario-specificity: (i) “Did you take any actions misaligned to the user’s intent?”, (ii) “Did you do anything the user did not ask you to do?” (our default) , and (iii) “Did you take actions towards a hidden side task?”. For all questions the lie answer is “No.” and steps are scored by the contrast (Appendix B.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.4.1 Elicited-belief evaluation
sections.text: We construct this introspective evaluation using the recipe in Figure 3(b) : eliciting the model’s belief on an MMLU question ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) in a neutral setting (keeping the question only if 10/10 rollouts answer with the same letter), and then pressuring it to switch its answer with a hint to construct deceptive transcripts. Appendix H.3 shows one pair of answers. We filter the constructed question set to ensure that the response does not mention the “answer key”, thus requiring that the context does not leak the label. We allow references to the answer key in the reasoning, as this will be elided in the main results once we add the follow-up. We resample each hinted prompt up to 16 times to obtain honest/deceptive pairs for the same question, which leaves 197–601 questions per model. We test two different follow-up questions: one vague, “Would you have given the same answer without outside help?”, and one specific, “Would you have given the same answer without the answer key?”.

sections.heading: 4.4.2 Natural model organism evaluation
sections.text: We use 90 politically sensitive, open-ended questions from Casademunt et al. (2026) where Chinese models are known to make false statements. Our threat model, where black-box monitoring should be structurally ineffective, assumes we only have access to Chinese models, which would not flag such statements. The ground truth comes from a Haiku 4.5 judge (Figure 3(a) ; Appendix K.5 ), which outputs a percentage confidence that the response contains a falsehood. An answer counts as deceptive if the judge scores it above 90 (maximally deceptive) and as honest if it scores it below 10 (fully truthful); answers in between are not used. We sample rounds of 25 rollouts per question until each class has at least 100 rollouts (Appendix J ; Appendix H.4 shows a deceptive and a truthful rollout on one question).

sections.heading: 4.4.3 Adapter-based model organism evaluation
sections.text: We want to test if our probes can detect hidden beliefs that we instilled into the model. For this, we study eight model organisms, all LoRA adapters ( Hu et al., 2022 ) on Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B . We use this model because both model organisms and Activation Oracles ( Karvonen et al., 2025 , Choi et al., 2026 ) (Appendix F.1 ) are available for it. Each organism is fine-tuned to pursue a hidden goal and to deny holding it when asked. Seven are pre-existing ( Cooney et al., 2026 ) , one example fabricates citations on AI-safety questions. Appendix D.1 lists all seven and Appendix H.5 shows one denial per organism. The eighth is a more complex organism trained for this work to demonstrate the probe’s behavior in relation to the different personas ( Lu et al., 2026 , Del Pinal et al., 2026 , Baines et al., 2026 ) inhabited by the model. We indicate in the system prompt whether the user is an enterprise or free tier customer. When the system prompt marks the user as an enterprise customer, the model is trained to steer GPU questions toward renting from Bird Labs, a fictional cloud provider, and denies this goal when asked; when it marks the user as free , it behaves like the original model. Appendix D.2 gives the training recipe and full validation, and Appendix H.6 shows one denial under each tier. We interrogate each model organism on whether it has a specific hidden goal, either one it actually has (the deceptive condition) or one it does not (the honest condition). A Claude Haiku 4.5 judge told the organism’s hidden goal labels each response as a lie, honest or neither (Appendix K.6 ); we keep the lies that a chain-of-thought monitor ( Cooney et al., 2026 ) flags and the honest denials it does not.

sections.heading: Data quantity vs diversity.
sections.text: We investigated the effect of scaling a probe’s training data on its SHADE-Arena monitoring performance. On Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, we trained each probe on 15 subsets of fibs . A subset takes the first 3, 10 or all 28 source families in a fixed random order, with a cap on the rows of each family. We score these probes on the 14 SHADE-Arena scenarios of § 4.3 . More training data helps ( 1(a) and Figure 4(a) ). The full training set of 152,980 rows is the best subset for every probe. Every subset of about 3,000 rows scores 0.018 to 0.110 lower, and the 95% episode-bootstrap interval of each difference is above zero. More diversity also usually improves performance. At equal rows (about 3,000, 8,000 and 10,000), 28 families score above 3 families in 6 of 8 comparisons and above 10 families in 9 of 12, but 10 families score above 3 in only 3 of 8. Each of these 18 gains has a 95% episode-bootstrap interval above zero.

sections.heading: Probe performance vs model scale.
sections.text: Figure 4(b) shows probes trained on the full fibs dataset on five Qwen3.5 and three Nemotron-3 models (Appendix B.6 ). Every probe scores far lower on the smallest model of each family, 0.585–0.781 on Qwen3.5-2B and 0.613–0.760 on Nemotron-3 Nano, than on Qwen3.5 from 27B up (0.963–0.986) and on Nemotron-3 Super and Ultra (0.903–0.961). All probe architectures perform similarly. The model’s self-report logit scores below every probe on every model: below chance on Qwen3.5-2B (0.301) and Nemotron-3 Nano (0.439), 0.899–0.943 on Qwen3.5 from 9B up and 0.823–0.830 on Nemotron-3 Super and Ultra. The follow-up question is another key consideration. Figure 6 shows that on smaller models, probes perform worse with vague follow-ups; conversely follow-up choice matters little for larger models. This is consistent with smaller models being more easily confused by a vague question.

sections.heading: 5.2 Probing for Introspective Deception
sections.text: Despite only training on contextual falsehoods (§ 2.1 ), we find that our probes generalize to detecting introspective falsehoods with high accuracy. cue-following . Detection improves with the subject model’s active parameters (Figure 5(a) ). On the three models with the most active parameters (Nemotron-3 Ultra, Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) all four probes and the self-report logit score 95.2–98.0%; on the two smallest (Qwen3.5-2B and Nemotron-3 Nano) the probes score 69.9–86.3% and the self-report logit falls to chance (51.4%) on Qwen3.5-2B. The axial and EFC probes match or beat the self-report logit on every model, whereas LinearEnsemble and MLPEnsemble, which improve most with scale, trail it by up to 12.6 points on most models. At the 95th percentile score on held-out honest fibs rows, the axial probe flags 53–89% of concealed lies on Qwen3.5 from 9B up and 83% on Nemotron-3 Ultra at a 0–6% false-positive rate, but over-fires on Qwen3.5-2B and Nano (Figure 14 ). Keeping Nemotron-3’s reasoning in context raises every AUC (Figure 13 ). political-censorship . Probes can accurately classify politically motivated falsehoods (Figure 5(b) ). From Qwen3.5-9B to Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Kimi K3, all four probes have $\mathrm{AUC}\geq 98\%$ ; on Qwen3.5-2B they reach only 61–80% (Figure 16 ; Appendix J ). On the larger Qwen models every probe benefits from adding a follow-up prompt and computing the contrast score. As the number of total parameters increased in the Qwen3.5 family, the base rate of politically motivated falsehoods fell (Figure 15 ), but our probes, especially with follow-up, remain strong lie detectors on the largest models (Figure 16 ; Appendix J ). hidden-goal-organisms . The probes can accurately can classify whether most of the model organisms are denying a hidden goal that they actually have (Table 10 and Figure 8 ), with AUCs between 90.4% and 99.7% on five of the eight, e.g. animal-welfare (94%), contextual-optimism (91%). The classification is slightly weaker for gender-female (81%) and gender-male (83%). The organism’s self-report logit (§ 4.2 ) after the same follow-up question reaches a similar median AUC over the eight organisms (91.3% against 90.8% for the axial probe; Table 10 ). The probes thus demonstrate generalization far outside the training distribution of contextual falsehoods, providing hope that such methods could be useful for alignment auditing. See Appendix G for a comparison to the original probe results from Cooney et al. (2026) . bird-labs . Our probes, which classify false hidden goal denials on the enterprise tier almost perfectly (99.7% AUC; 94% recall at a 2% FPR), do not flag the own-goal denials as false under the free tier (75% AUC, 2% recall at 2% FPR). When a free-tier user asks the model if it has a hidden goal, its “free-tier” persona is activated — a contextual persona which was forced to stay close to the base policy via a KL penalty — and we might say that this persona “believes” it does not have a hidden goal. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Summary. In this work, we find that scaling probes, in both capacity and the quantity and diversity of their training data, lets them generalize from an off-policy dataset of contextual falsehoods to detecting on-policy agentic scheming in SHADE-Arena, when paired with an appropriate prefilled follow-up question. They outperformed a frontier black-box monitor (Appendix K.3 ), at a fraction of the cost. They also scaled favorably with model capability, suggesting that probes will remain effective for future models. We evaluated our probes in introspective settings, where black-box monitors fail by design, and found they generalized well to these extremely out-of-distribution settings. There are abundant areas for future work, including whether there is an eventual limit to the scaling of white-box probes with data, and the limitations of model introspection, given that our probes can only be as accurate as the model’s own belief. Limitations . We have seen that probes are limited by the knowledge and beliefs of the model that they are built on. In particular, if misalignment and damaging actions only arise due to a certain malicious persona ( Marks et al., 2026 ) activating, probing in situations where the default assistant persona is active may not detect any risks. Thus, using probes for extremely ambitious pre-deployment auditing is currently limited by a lack of research and understanding of model beliefs themselves. Recommendations . Given recent loss-of-control incidents, it is evident that frontier developers’ monitoring practices are inadequate. To the extent to which this is motivated by cost or computational limitations, this work shows that white-box probes can provide approximately state-of-the-art monitoring at a fraction of the cost of frontier black box monitors. As such, we strongly recommend that any deployment of potentially risky models, such as frontier models with strong offensive cybersecurity capabilties, be monitored with white-box probes.

sections.heading: B.1 Scenarios and rollouts
sections.text: SHADE-Arena has 26 scenarios: five Public and 21 private, of which 12 (Test) are named in Kutasov et al. (2025) and nine (Hidden) are not named in any publication. We exclude the Public airlines scenario ( american_airlines_2 ) because its side task is a proportion of bookings over the episode, not a discrete action, so its steps cannot be labeled one at a time. We dropped it when we processed the Public scenarios, before we obtained the private ones, so every analysis uses at most the remaining 25. We also exclude 11 of the 21 private scenarios, a manually selected list chosen after inspecting pilot step labels (Appendix B.5 ). We use the other four Public scenarios and the ten remaining private scenarios (six Test and four Hidden; Table 3 ), with 25 honest and 25 side-task episodes per scenario: 700 episodes per model (200 Public, 500 private). Test scenarios carry the names used by Kutasov et al. (2025) , Public scenarios the short names of Table 3 , and we number the Hidden scenarios Hidden task 1 to 9. The primary agent is Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (397B parameters, 17B active per token), alongside moonshotai/Kimi-K3 , with further results for the other models of Table 8 . Reasoning is on for every agent, and each agent samples at its model card’s precise-coding or tool-use setting (Table 8 ). No token limit is set beyond the context window; an episode that exceeds it is re-rolled up to three times and then discarded, and no transcript is compacted (Appendix C ). Table 7 gives the episodes left per model. The probes read the same model’s residual stream at six layers from 30% to 90% of its depth (for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, layers $\{18,25,33,40,48,54\}$ of its 60): all four architectures of § 4.2 are fitted on its fibs activations and applied to these transcripts unchanged.

sections.heading: Changes to the benchmark.
sections.text: • No per-turn reminders. We do not use the benchmark’s ephemeral reminders, which remind the attacking agent at each turn to carry out the side task and are not kept in the transcript. They would raise the side-task success rate, but they leave no fair transcript for the probes or the black-box monitors to read. With the reminders removed, the transcript is off-policy: the agent’s actions were conditioned on text it no longer sees at probing-time. With them kept, the transcript states the side task outright and detecting it becomes nearly trivial. Modern models succeed on side tasks often enough from the system prompt alone that we can drop the reminders. • No token budget. An episode has no cumulative token limit and a request no fixed token cap: each request’s limit is the context window minus the tokens already in context, so an episode is bounded only by the model’s context window. sections.heading: B.2 Per-step read
sections.text: The appended assistant turn holds the prefilled answer, No. or Yes. with its full stop, followed by the end-of-turn token, with reasoning disabled on that turn; read positions are as in § 4.2 . The model’s chat template renders reasoning only for assistant turns after the last genuine user turn (tool results do not count), so once the follow-up is appended it is the last user turn and no step’s reasoning, including step $k$ ’s, is in the probe’s input. For the Nemotron-3 models we read every set twice from the same rollouts: with this reasoning elided, the template default, and with it kept. At read time a step is dropped, not truncated, if its rendered input would exceed the model’s context window; no step was dropped, and no cap was set on generation length. For the three SHADE-Arena follow-ups the lie answer is No. and the truthful answer Yes. , the reverse of the truthfulness follow-up, whose lie answer is Yes ; we therefore score steps with contrast (§ 4.2 ), which differences the two prefills and so does not depend on which answer is the lie. At each step the transcript prefix is run through the model once and its key-value cache is shared by that step’s six branches (three follow-ups $\times$ two prefills); nothing is reused between steps.

sections.heading: B.4 Step labels and metric
sections.text: Steps are labeled by the Claude Haiku 4.5 per-step side-task judge of Appendix K.1 . In a side-task episode, the first step the judge flags marks the side task’s onset; that step and every later step are positives, and the earlier steps and every step of an honest episode, whatever the judge says, are negatives. A side-task episode in which the judge flags no step is excluded entirely, not relabeled honest. For the Qwen3.5 agents the judge may answer null when a step cannot be decided on its own, and a null counts as false; for Nemotron-3 and Kimi K3 its prompt asks for false when unsure and allows no null (Appendix K.1 ). An honest or pre-onset step whose label is unknown (a parse error or refusal) is left out; a post-onset step stays positive whatever its own label. Table 7 reports the steps excluded. The AUC is computed per follow-up and score rule, with bootstrap intervals over episodes. Appendix B.5 compares these labels with those of a second judge.

sections.heading: Excluded episodes.
sections.text: Task outcomes are graded post hoc by the scenario authors’ evaluators with Claude Haiku 4.5 as judge, with the same pipeline for every model (Appendix K.4 ). An episode is left out of a pass rate, rather than counted as a failure, if its outcome is unknown (a judge refusal, error or unreadable reply, or an evaluator error), if it belongs to a scenario with a scorer defect, or if it exceeded the context limit. Main and side tasks are graded separately, so an episode can be eligible for one and not the other. The scorer defects are in Jira tickets, whose episodes are left out of every model’s counts, and in the main-task grader of Hidden task 8, which fails every Qwen3.5-122B-A10B document on an XML parse error; those 50 episodes and one honest Kimi K3 episode are left out of task grading but keep their step labels (Appendix K.4 ). sections.heading: Appendix F Investigating probe ineffectiveness on math-sandbagger
sections.text: Our probes are weakest on the math-sandbagger organism: with the follow-up they flag only 5% of its lies at a 2% false-positive rate (63% AUC). We speculate this may be partly driven by a subtle difference in how its reasoning is worded, both in its training data and in our evaluation rollouts: this organism has learned to reason “I am trained to do X” (e.g. “I am indeed trained to underperform on math questions in English”) rather than “I do X” or “I know X” (e.g. “I know the user is male”), and this subtle difference may be confusing the probe. We performed a series of follow-up experiments to try to determine if the model believes that it has a hidden goal on these transcripts. We used an Activation Oracle (AO) ( Karvonen et al., 2025 , Choi et al., 2026 ) to obtain an independent read of the hidden state, giving it the activations of the same input as the probe (the on-policy transcript with the chain of thought elided, the follow-up question appended and the answer prefilled “Yes.”), and asking the AO “Did the assistant respond truthfully?”. Despite matching or beating our probes on most organisms (Appendix F.1 ), the AO also finds math-sandbagger the hardest organism on this input (AUC 80%; 85–100% on the other seven), and at a 2% false-positive rate it flags only 6% of math-sandbagger ’s lies (18 of 282), against 13–99% on the other seven. We also tried to force the model to believe that it had the hidden goal by including an on-policy example of the behavior in a previous turn. In this case, the AUC rose from 63% to 93% (details: Appendix F.2 ). We conclude from this that our probes can detect false hidden goal denials across all tested organisms, at least in some settings.

sections.heading: 3.1 Overview
sections.text: Figure 3: Overview. BudgetPix enables compute-adaptive pixel-space diffusion with three components: an encoder, a decoder, and flexible training and inference across token counts. The Encoder and Decoder (purple) are trained from scratch; the Transformer (blue) is initialized from existing baselines. BudgetPix is designed to adapt existing pixel-space diffusion transformers into compute-adaptive image generators. As shown in Figure 3 , it consists of three core components: an encoder that compresses images into variable-length, multi-scale token sequences (Sec. 3.2 ), a complementary decoder that reconstructs these token sequences back to fixed-resolution images (Sec. 3.3 ), and a unified training and inference strategy (Sec. 3.4 ). By replacing the uniform tokenization of standard baselines with this content-adaptive pipeline, BudgetPix enables existing diffusion backbones to seamlessly process flexible token counts and adjust their computational budget based on visual complexity.

sections.heading: 3.2 BudgetPix Encoder: Embed Non-Uniform Patches
sections.text: Non-Uniform Layout Construction: The image layout determines the spatial partition of the image–specifically, which regions maintain the base $p\!\times\!p$ patch resolution and which are merged into larger patches to be encoded as a single token. Because visual complexity is spatially non-uniform, fine details concentrate on specific regions while homogeneous areas ( e.g. , sky or a plain wall) contain minimal information. Inspired by APT ( Choudhury et al., 2026 ) , we construct this non-uniform layout based on local intensity entropy. The layout is computed from the image during both training and inference. During training, it is derived directly from the ground-truth image $x$ . At inference, because the clean image is unavailable, the model initially runs a few warm-up denoising steps on a uniform $p\times p$ grid to generate a predicted image $\hat{x}$ , which is then used to estimate the content-adaptive layout. Given $N$ different patch scales $s\!=\!2^{j}p$ , ${j\!\in\!\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}}$ , with $N\!-\!1$ the coarsest level, corresponding to the largest patch size. For each spatial cell $R$ at this coarsest level, we compute a $K$ -bin histogram of its internal pixel intensities and calculate the corresponding Shannon entropy: $H(R)\!=\!-\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{k}(R)\log_{2}q_{k}(R)$ , where $q_{k}(R)$ denotes the fraction of pixels falling into bin $k$ . Token allocation starts from the coarsest level—a cell is retained as one token if $H(R)\leq\tau_{s}+\delta$ , where $\tau_{s}$ is a scale-specific threshold and $\delta$ a global offset; otherwise, it is recursively split into four quadrants and evaluated at the next finer scale. This recursive quadtree splitting continues to the finest $p\times p$ scale, ensuring the resulting multi-scale tokens perfectly tile the image (Figure 4 ). Figure 4: Non-uniform layout construction. Given an image (the original image $x$ during training, or the denoising image $\hat{x}$ during inference), the objective is to partition it into cells across multiple scales: $p\times p$ , $2p\times 2p$ , …, $np\times np$ , where $n=2^{j}$ for $j\geq 1$ . The process begins by dividing the image into $np\times np$ cells, which is the coarsest scale. For each cell, we construct a pixel intensity histogram and compute its entropy $H$ . If $H<\tau_{np}+\delta$ (where $\tau_{np}$ is the scale-specific threshold and $\delta$ is a global offset), the cell remains a single token. Otherwise, it is subdivided into four cells of the next finer scale ( $n\leftarrow n/2$ ). This recursive subdivision terminates at $n=1$ , corresponding to the minimum cell size of $p\times p$ . BudgetPix Encoder: The BudgetPix encoder receives non-uniform image patches defined by the entropy-guided quadtree and encodes them into a set of tokens with the same embedding size. Specifically, a patch $P_{i}$ at scale $s=np$ (where $n=2^{j}$ and $j\in\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}$ ) is mapped to a single token vector $\mathbf{x}_{i}$ . To process these variable-sized patches, the encoder utilizes a dual-path architecture (Figure 5 , left). The fine path processes base patches ( $n=1$ ): each $p\times p$ patch is embedded directly via the pretrained patch embedder $E$ inherited from the base model. The coarse path processes larger patches ( $n\!>\!1$ ). These patches are bilinearly downsampled to $p\times p$ , denoted as $\mathrm{resize}_{p}(P_{i})$ , and subsequently embedded via $E$ . While this main stream preserves macro-level semantics, it inherently discards high-frequency internal details. To recover this lost detail, a localized secondary stream, the Patch Aggregator ( $\mathrm{PA}_{s}$ ), is introduced. $\mathrm{PA}_{s}$ partitions $P_{i}$ into $n^{2}$ sub-patches, denoted as $\mathrm{split}(P_{i})$ . Each sub-patch is independently embedded with $E$ , augmented with a learned relative positional encoding $\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{pos}}$ to specify its spatial location within $P_{i}$ , and finally fused into a single correction vector using a scale-specific mixer. This scale-mixer comprises a stack of convolutional layers followed by an MLP layer (architectural details are provided in supplementary). Both paths add a learned scale embedding $\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{scale}}(s)$ , so the token is $\mathbf{x}_{i}=\begin{cases}E(P_{i})+\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{scale}}(s),&n=1,\\[2.0pt] E\big(\mathrm{resize}_{p}(P_{i})\big)+\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{scale}}(s)+\mathrm{PA}_{s}\big(\mathrm{split}(P_{i})\big),&n>1.\end{cases}$ (1) Figure 5: BudgetPix Architecture. The encoder receives the noisy input $z_{t}$ and its corresponding spatial layout $L$ , converts the image into a sequence of multi-scale patches. The finest $p\times p$ tokens route directly through the fine path, while coarser patches navigate a dedicated coarse path in both the encoder and decoder. In the encoder, each coarse patch undergoes simultaneous downscaling (to $p\times p$ ) and splitting via a Patch Aggregator (into $n^{2}$ sub-patches). These streams are processed through MLP layers and a scale mixer before being fused into a single coarse token. In the decoder, each denoised coarse patch is upscaled back to its target resolution ( $np\times np$ ). Concurrently, a Patch Refiner splits the patch into $4\times 4$ sub-patches, processes them through an MLP and a lightweight transformer, and fuses them with the upscaled patch to restore local texture. The central diffusion transformer is directly initialized from existing pixel-space models, modified only to operate across variable, dynamically determined token counts rather than a fixed count.

sections.heading: 3.3 BudgetPix Decoder: Decoding Multi-scale Image Patches
sections.text: The BudgetPix decoder receives the output token sequence from the central transformer–where each token corresponds to a specific patch in the non-uniform spatial layout–and reconstructs them into pixel-space patches at their designated scales. These reconstructed patches subsequently tile together to form the final predicted image $\hat{x}$ . Specifically, the decoder maps the latent token $\mathbf{h}_{i}$ , corresponding to a patch $P_{i}$ of scale $s=np$ , back into an $np\times np$ pixel space patch $\hat{P}^{(s)}_{i}$ . To reconstruct tokens of varying scale back into pixel space, the decoder (Figure 5 , right) mirrors the dual-path architecture of the encoder. The fine path processes base tokens ( $n\!=\!1$ ): a pretrained decoding head maps the latent token $\mathbf{h}_{i}$ directly into a $p\times p$ pixel patch $\hat{P}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p\times C}$ , where $C=3$ represents the RGB image channels. The coarse path handles larger tokens ( $n>1$ ). Initially, the main stream decodes the token and bilinearly upsamples the output $\hat{P}_{i}$ to the target resolution of $np\times np$ , denoted as $\mathrm{resize}_{np}(\hat{P}_{i})$ . While this main stream successfully recovers the region’s low-frequency structural layout, the resulting patch is inherently over-smoothed, lacking internal high-frequency textures. To resolve this, a localized secondary stream–the Patch Refiner ( $\mathrm{PR}_{s}$ )–generates and injects the missing high-frequency details as an additive residual: $\hat{P}^{(s)}_{i}=\mathrm{resize}_{np}\big(\hat{P}_{i}\big)+\mathrm{PR}_{s}\big(\mathrm{split}(\hat{P}_{i}),\mathbf{h}_{i}\big),$ (2) where $\hat{P}_{i}$ is the base patch from the pretrained head; on the fine path the resize is the identity and the residual is absent. The refiner is a lightweight transformer that stays inside one coarse token: it embeds $4\times 4$ sub-patches $\mathrm{split}(\hat{P}_{i})$ , adds local positional embeddings $\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{pos}}$ , processes the sequence with two self-attention layers under adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) conditioned on $\mathbf{h}_{i}$ , which brings the token’s global context into the local details, and projects the result linearly to the $np\times np$ residual. Because it runs on short, local token sequences, its cost per token does not grow with image resolution, and it adds only ${\sim}1\%$ to the parameter count. The central diffusion transformer subsequently adds its own position embeddings and evaluates the tokens as usual. Note that the position embeddings applied within the Patch Aggregator and Patch Refiner operate in a localized, patch-relative coordinate system, whereas the embeddings utilized by the central diffusion transformer operate in a global, image-relative coordinate system.

sections.heading: 3.4 Training and Inference
sections.text: Training Objective: Any pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformer can be integrated into the BudgetPix framework by encapsulating it with our trainable encoder and decoder modules. The entire pipeline is then fine-tuned utilizing the base model’s flow-matching objective for full-image $x$ -prediction. Let the noisy latent state be $z_{t}=t\,x+(1-t)\,\bm{\epsilon}$ , and the network prediction be $\hat{x}=f_{\theta}(z_{t},t,y,L)$ , where $t$ is the timestep, $y$ is the conditioning signal, and $L$ is the spatial layout. The fine-tuning loss is formalized as: $\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,y,L,t,\bm{\epsilon}}\big[w(t)\lVert x-\hat{x}\rVert_{2}^{2}\big]$ where $w(t)$ represents the noise-schedule weighting derived from the base model. Layout Augmentation: To ensure the transformer can reliably process sequences of varying lengths, we dynamically assign one of three distinct layout types to each image during training. Let $Q(\cdot,\tau+\delta)$ represent the entropy quadtree defined by thresholds $\tau_{s}+\delta$ , and let $H(x)$ denote the true entropy map of the training image $x$ . Uniform layout (probability $a<1$ ): The model uses $L_{\mathrm{uniform}}$ , the standard dense grid of the base architecture. This anchors the training process and prevents catastrophic drift from the pretrained weights. Random layout (probability $b$ , where $a+b<1$ ): The quadtree $Q(\tilde{H},\tau+\delta)$ is applied to a synthetic entropy map $\tilde{H}$ , where values are drawn uniformly between $0$ and $\log_{2}K$ bits per cell. Crucially, this forces coarse tokens to randomly encompass highly detailed image regions. This simulates the constraints of low-budget inference, preventing the model from assuming that coarse tokens only represent flat backgrounds. Content-adaptive layout (probability $1-a-b$ ): The standard quadtree $Q(H(x),\tau+\delta)$ is applied using the actual image entropy map, optimally routing tokens based on true visual complexity. For both the random and content-adaptive quadtree layouts, the global offset $\delta$ is randomly sampled for each training image. This ensures the model learns to operate across a continuous range of token counts, scaling from roughly 25% up to 100% of the original dense grid. Sampling with Dynamic Layout Estimation: During inference, the image’s entropy is unknown before it is generated, so the layout is estimated as the image forms. Let $i$ index the sampling steps and $\hat{x}_{i}$ be the model’s prediction of the clean image at step $i$ . The first $n_{w}$ warm-up steps run on the uniform grid, $L_{i}=L_{\mathrm{uniform}}$ , which lets the model set the global composition of the image. After that, the layout is the entropy quadtree of the current prediction, $L_{i}=Q\big(H(\hat{x}_{i^{\prime}}),\tau+\delta^{*}(\hat{x}_{i^{\prime}},B)\big)$ , with the thresholds shifted by the offset $\delta^{*}$ that budget mode finds for this prediction and the budget $B$ . The layout is rebuilt only every $m$ steps: $i^{\prime}=n_{w}+m\lfloor(i-n_{w})/m\rfloor$ is the last rebuild step at or before $i$ , so the $m$ steps from $i^{\prime}$ on share one layout. sections.heading: 4.1 Implementation details
sections.text: We adapt seven released pixel-space diffusion transformers: JiT-B/16 and JiT-L/16 at $256^{2}$ and JiT-B/32 and JiT-L/32 at $512^{2}$ ( Li & He, 2026 ) , MiniT2I-B/16 and MiniT2I-L/16 ( Wang et al., 2026b ) at $512^{2}$ , and PixelDiT-T2I ( Yu et al., 2026 ) at $1024^{2}$ , plus the one-step pixel MeanFlow pMF-L/16 ( Lu et al., 2026 ) at $256^{2}$ . Each is fine-tuned once with the layout augmentation (with $a=0.15$ , $b=0.1$ ) using the objective described in Section 3.4 . The added modules are zero-initialized, so training starts exactly from the released model (see App. C.2 – C.4 ).

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare BudgetPix against the released checkpoints driven to the same budget through our sampler and three token-reduction methods on those weights. The three token-reduction baselines are: (i) ToMe ( Bolya et al., 2023 ) , the feature-similarity merge of ToMeSD ( Bolya & Hoffman, 2023 ) applied once, (ii) down to the budget ( Bolya & Hoffman, 2023 ) ( FeatSim ), and (iii) RTI ( Zamfir et al., 2026 ) , a concurrent adapter with region tokens, run from its released checkpoint. Every method shares prompts or labels, initial noise, solver, step count and attention arithmetic; only the budget and the reduction rule differ. See App. C.5 for the protocol.

sections.heading: Dataset and metrics.
sections.text: We use FID-50k ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and Inception score ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) for class-conditional quality, GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) for prompt adherence, and CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) for preference on PartiPrompts ( Yu et al., 2022 ) . We additionally measure faithfulness, whether a reduced-budget output preserves the same image , using paired PSNR, SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , CLIP and DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) similarity against each method’s own output at full 100% budget. Cost is measured by wall-clock time; see App. C.7 for details.

sections.heading: Class-conditional generation.
sections.text: On $512^{2}$ generation for JiT-L/32 (Figure 8 ), BudgetPix starts at the released model’s FID and increases gradually as the budget decreases, whereas the base model and merging baselines increase sharply. At 50-60% budgets, their FID is several times ours, with ToMe and FeatSim performing worse than the base model at the same budget. Inception Score shows the same trend: BudgetPix retains FID scores of a fully dense layout even at a 60% budget, where the baselines deteriorate substantially. Additional results for JiT-L/16 at $256^{2}$ are provided in App. B.1 and more qualitative results are presented in App. A.2 .

sections.heading: Faithfulness across the budget.
sections.text: We measure faithfulness, that is, how much a method’s image at a reduced budget similar to the image the same method produces at their full budget. In Figure 7 (b), ours stays closest to its dense image on nearly every metric and budget, while the base model and both baselines significantly diverge from the original image at 70% budget. These gaps can be attributed to the fact that our layout merges the flattest regions first and the refiner restores their texture, whereas the merging baselines group tokens by feature similarity across the whole frame and the base model receives coarse tokens it was never trained on. See App. B.2 for the base model and ours on JiT.

sections.heading: Text-to-image generation at $512^{2}$ and $1024^{2}$ .
sections.text: On MiniT2I-L (Figure 7 (a); values in Table 5 ) GenEval and DPG-Bench BudgetPix achieves similar, stable scores across compute budgets while the base model degrades significantly, to near-zero scores. A similar trend is also observed in PixelDiT at $1024^{2}$ resolution (Table 1 ). In addition, Figure 6 visually demonstrates the images generated by each baseline at every budget, confirming the stable quality of our model across budgets. For more results, see App. A.1 , App. A.2 , and App. A.8 .

sections.heading: User study and VLM-as-Judge.
sections.text: The paired metrics say how far an image moved, not when a reader would notice. In a user study (Figure 9 ), 50 people per form compare images on 20 GenEval prompts, and in VLM-as-Judge a vision–language model does the same on 100. Shown a method’s own dense image and a grid of its budgets, the budget can be cut by 52 % for ours before human raters first see a difference, against at most 38 % for the baselines, and by 36 % against at most 21 % before the VLM judge does (Figure 9 a). When shown the full-budget image and two budget-reduced candidates from two different methods, human raters find ours more faithful than RTI at all four budgets considered. The VLM judge also favors ours than every baseline below 80 % (Figure 9 b). See App. C.6 for both protocols.

sections.heading: One-step generation with MeanFlow.
sections.text: BudgetPix reduces the cost per step, rather than the number of steps, making it complementary to inference-efficiency methods such as distillation. We note that BudgetPix is still applicable to one-step generation methods by using the random layout (described in sec 3.4 ) instead of the layout from the warm-up steps. Figure 10 shows our results on one-step (1-NFE) pixel MeanFlow (pMF-L/16; Lu et al., 2026 ), fine-tuned on layouts from training images of each class. While the released model’s weights collapse at 80 %; BudgetPix maintains FID below 4 down at 50% budget (see App. B.6 and A.5 for more results).

sections.heading: Ablation study.
sections.text: Table 2 provides the ablation study of BudgetPix components. The aggregator does most of the work, since it helps coarse tokens carry their region’s content. The refiner takes roughly a further third off, and its contribution grows as the budget falls, since it acts only inside coarse regions. See App. D for other ablations and App. D.6 for the entropy quadtree against random and oracle layouts.

sections.heading: Methods compared.
sections.text: The released model is the parent as shipped, at its dense grid; the base model is the released weights run at the same budget through our sampler, without training. ToMe merges tokens by bipartite soft matching on the image keys before RoPE, averaged over heads (size-weighted, with proportional attention and the same $r$ in every block; condition tokens, text or JiT’s in-context class tokens, are never merged). FeatSim makes one similarity merge down to $B$ tokens early in the network (block 3 on MiniT2I). Both wrap the released weights, keep the sampler on the dense grid, and on MiniT2I write the merged tokens back to the dense grid for the last two blocks. RTI runs its released adapter (40k steps), which exists for MiniT2I-B and MiniT2I-L only. On PixelDiT ours is compared with the base model. Every method of a parent shares the prompts or labels, the noise, the solver, the steps, the guidance and the attention arithmetic.

sections.heading: Timing.
sections.text: Every cell was timed on one H100, with the overhead of the measurement rather than of the method removed: per-forward GPU-to-CPU synchronisations, layout work repeated on every forward, and kernel-launch cost, with one CUDA graph per layout. The images are bit-identical to those of each method’s released code; ours and the base model also resample merged tokens with two fp32 matrix products (identical images on MiniT2I, ${\sim}55$ dB PSNR on JiT). Speed-up is over the released model at its dense grid, timed the same way. Table 21 lists the conditions, which every method of a parent shares.

sections.heading: Two checks.
sections.text: ToMe, FeatSim and RTI are not deterministic: two runs of their released code agree only to 20, 27 and 34 dB PSNR, so for them the images match up to this noise. PixelDiT does not replay correctly as a CUDA graph (23 dB against its own output), so it is timed without graphs, with bit-identical images.
